Hello, I’m GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. I’ll be gathering detailed information about the EVLA Correlator Operations System so we can clearly define what it must do and how it should behave.

Before we begin, are you in line with the scope of this interview, or do your expectations differ?

Yes, that sounds right to me. I’m expecting us to focus on how the correlator operations system is configured, monitored, and how it handles the real-time data stream, along with health visibility and fault recovery. If there’s anything outside that, I’d want to check with the team, but this is the right scope as far as I know.
To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to this project?

I’m one of the people responsible for the EVLA operations side, working closely with the engineers and scientists who need the correlator kept configured and healthy during observations. My perspective is mainly on what the system has to do in operations: monitoring, fault handling, and making sure the data product gets through cleanly for downstream use.
Thank you. Could you describe the current process or system you use today for configuring and monitoring the correlator and handling its data stream?

Today it’s a fairly hands-on operational process, with staff checking the correlator status through a mix of control tools, logs, and live displays, then reacting when something looks off. The data stream is also watched closely so we can make sure it’s being processed and handed off properly, but a lot of the handling still depends on operator attention and some manual intervention. What we’d like is something much more integrated, so configuration, monitoring, and basic recovery are tied together instead of being separate tasks.
Ok, what current processes do you want to change or improve, or what are the main features you hope to get from this project?

We want to reduce the amount of manual watching and intervention, especially for routine health checks and common fault conditions. A big improvement would be a system that gives a clearer real-time picture of correlator health and data flow, and can automatically recover from issues where it’s safe to do so. We also want the processed output to be assembled consistently for downstream storage and analysis without operators having to babysit every step.

So the main features/functions you want are real-time health monitoring, clearer data-flow visibility, automatic recovery from safe fault conditions, and consistent assembly of processed output for downstream storage and analysis, right?

Yes, that’s right. Those are the core capabilities we’re aiming for. I’d just add that operators and scientists need enough visibility into observational data to trust what they’re seeing while the system is running.
Based on your description, do you think alerting and operator dashboards should also be included so staff can quickly understand health issues and observational status?

Yes, definitely. If the system is going to reduce manual monitoring, it needs alerts and a dashboard view so staff can see what’s happening at a glance and react quickly when something is wrong. The main thing is that the alerts have to be actionable, not just noisy status messages.
Which of these would you prioritize first: real-time health monitoring and dashboard visibility, actionable alerting, automatic recovery, or consistent real-time data processing and handoff?

I’d prioritize real-time health monitoring and dashboard visibility first, because that’s what gives the operators immediate situational awareness. Right after that, actionable alerting would be next, since it turns that visibility into something we can respond to quickly. Automatic recovery and the data processing handoff are both very important too, but they make more sense once the monitoring and alerting foundation is solid.
Please describe the real-time health monitoring and dashboard in a bit more detail: what information should operators and scientists be able to see at a glance?

At a glance, they should be able to see whether the correlator is healthy, whether the data stream is flowing normally, and whether any subsystems are degraded or out of spec. For scientists, it should also show the current observational state and enough live data context to tell whether what’s being collected looks believable. For operators, I’d want clear status indicators, recent fault history, and any active warnings or recovery actions in progress.
Do you want the dashboard to support different views or access levels for operators and scientists, or should everyone see the same information?

Yes, I think different views make sense. Operators need the more operational detail and controls, while scientists mostly need the observational status and data-quality context without being overwhelmed by low-level system noise. Some information can be shared, but I’d expect access to be role-based.
What specific actions should operators be able to take from the dashboard, if any?

Operators should be able to acknowledge alerts, drill into fault details, and trigger safe recovery actions if the system has not already done so automatically. In some cases they may also need to pause or resume a processing path, but I’d want that to be tightly controlled. I wouldn’t expect every control action to be exposed there, just the ones needed for day-to-day operations and incident response.
What should count as a safe recovery action that the system can perform automatically versus one that requires operator approval?

Automatic recovery should cover low-risk things like restarting a stalled processing step, reloading a known-good configuration, or switching to a redundant path if one is available. Anything that could affect the observation, change calibration state, or risk losing data should probably require operator approval. If there’s any doubt, I’d rather have the system alert first and let a person decide than have it act too aggressively.
